Macrovascular: coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, stroke. Chronic complications are split by vessel size. Microvascular: neuropathy, nephropathy and retinopathy. Macrovascular: coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease and stroke. Pioglitazone (Actos) and rosiglitazone (Avandia) are PPAR-gamma agonists. PPAR-gamma is a nuclear receptor, mostly in adipose tissue, that switches on genes of glucose and lipid metabolism. The result is more fat cells and fat mass, more fatty acid uptake into fat, and better insulin sensitivity in muscle and liver. 2 Choosing an insulin: rapid or regular for a meal, long-acting as basal, and the onset, peak and duration of each preparation Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Rapid-acting (analogs) Lispro (Humalog), aspart (NovoLog), glulisine (Apidra) Onset 5 to 15 minutes; lasts about 4 hours Mealtime (bolus), as needed Inhaled, very rapid Afrezza Acts within 1 to 2 minutes Mealtime Short-acting (regular, human) Humulin R, Novolin R Peaks about 3 hours; gone by about 8 hours Before meals; no prescription needed Intermediate (NPH, human) Humulin N, Novolin N Onset 2 to 4 hours; protamine slows absorption Longer coverage; no prescription needed Long-acting (analogs) Glargine (Lantus, Basaglar), detemir (Levemir) Slow, steady release, no real peak; glargine lasts more than 24 hours Basal, once daily Ultra-long Degludec (Tresiba); glargine as Toujeo Degludec lasts more than 42 hours Basal 3 Which drugs cause hypoglycemia (insulin and the secretagogues) and which rarely do Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Metformin has no effect at normal glucose, so its hypoglycemia risk is very low. Crucially, metformin has no effect in normoglycemic states. Insulin and the secretagogues lower glucose whatever it is; metformin won't bring a normal glucose lower. So its risk of hypoglycemia is very low, and it is weight neutral or causes modest weight loss. 4 Weight effects: gain with insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides and TZDs; loss with GLP-1 agonists; a GLP-1 agonist first for a patient with a weight problem Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank Insulin Yes Gain Sulfonylureas and meglitinides Yes Gain Metformin No Neutral or modest loss Thiazolidinediones No Gain GLP-1 agonists No (alone) Loss DPP-4 inhibitors No Neutral SGLT2 inhibitors Rare Not discussed Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors No No weight gain 5 Metformin: first-line, mechanism, no effect at normal glucose, GI upset, B12, lactic acidosis, eGFR below 30 Flagged in the recording · 7 questions in the bank Adverse effects: GI upset (nausea and vomiting, indigestion, cramps, bloating, diarrhea), which usually fades in one or two weeks; decreased vitamin B12 absorption, so some patients need B12 injections monthly or every 3 months; and lactic acidosis. Contraindications: an eGFR below 30, which is absolute, and acute or chronic metabolic acidosis. Cautions: excessive alcohol, unstable or acute heart failure, and hepatic impairment. When metformin is no longer enough after a few years, other drugs are added on. 6 Situational choice with heart failure, heart disease or kidney disease: avoid TZDs (edema, macular edema), consider an SGLT2 inhibitor or semaglutide, sitagliptin the DPP-4 exception, linagliptin without renal adjustment Flagged in the recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this TZDs cause edema and heart failure; contraindicated in NYHA class III or IV. Thiazolidinediones are the class linked to macular edema. Their signature problem is edema, which is dose-related, with weight gain and new or worsened heart failure, since peripheral and pulmonary edema are what heart failure looks like. They are contraindicated in NYHA class III or IV heart failure, and are now recommended only for patients without cardiovascular problems. They also raise the risk of macular edema; the professor said he skipped it in class, but it is on the slide. Avoid them when ALT is more than 2.5 times the upper limit of normal. Advantages: a low risk of hypoglycemia, preserved beta-cell function, higher HDL, and lower triglycerides and blood pressure. Advantages: no hypoglycemia, weight neutral, well tolerated, no renal adjustment for linagliptin, and usable in kidney and liver dysfunction. Disadvantages: expense, modest A1C lowering, low durability (about 2 years), and avoid in heart failure, except sitagliptin. 7 SGLT2 inhibitors: glucosuria, genital yeast infections, UTIs, hypotension, boxed warning for amputation Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank The adverse effects follow from the sugary urine and the water it pulls along (osmotic diuresis): genital fungal (yeast) infections in men and women, urinary tract infections, polyuria, and dizziness and hypotension from the lower circulating volume. Hyperkalemia is also listed: in the professor's words, when you lose sodium through these transporters, you tend to keep potassium. The warnings: fracture risk, lower bone mineral density (canagliflozin), bladder cancer (dapagliflozin), rare euglycemic DKA, acute kidney injury (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin), and a boxed warning for amputation, below the knee (canagliflozin, ertugliflozin), which was significant in clinical trials. 8 GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors: incretin actions, exendin-4, boxed warning for thyroid tumors, delayed gastric emptying Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this All GLP-1 agonists carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors. Side effects: nausea and vomiting, dose-dependent and fading with time; delayed gastric emptying, which can slow the absorption of drugs that need rapid absorption, such as oral contraceptives and antibiotics; rare pancreatitis; and acute renal failure. All carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors seen in animal studies, so people with a history of thyroid cancer are advised not to take them. Advantages: a low risk of hypoglycemia as monotherapy, weight loss and preserved beta-cell function. Disadvantages: expense, injection (with the extra cost of pen needles for daily forms), and poor tolerance in some people. Oral semaglutide (Rybelsus) is the one tablet; because it is poorly absorbed, the daily oral dose is far larger than the weekly injected one. Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) is now also approved for patients with cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease, and tirzepatide (Zepbound) for sleep apnea. 9 Secretagogues: the K-ATP channel mechanism, the need for working beta cells (C-peptide), low durability, sulfonylurea warnings Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank Secretagogues make the pancreas secrete insulin. A sulfonylurea binds the sulfonylurea receptor (SUR) on the beta cell's ATP-sensitive potassium channel and closes it. Potassium is trapped, the membrane depolarizes, voltage-gated calcium channels open, and the calcium influx causes exocytosis of insulin the cell has already made. This stimulation is continuous, whatever the glucose level. Two consequences follow. First, secretagogues only work in a patient whose pancreas can still make insulin: if beta cells have stopped, it doesn't matter how much you stimulate them. Second, they share insulin's side effects: hypoglycemia and weight gain. They also have low durability: after a year or two the dose has to go up, and eventually they stop working, because there is a limit to how far the pancreas can be squeezed. Other adverse effects are agranulocytosis, jaundice, nausea and vomiting, and hypersensitivity, since some people react to sulfur drugs. 10 Hypoglycemia in the dental chair: fast sugar by mouth if awake, glucagon in an emergency Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank Know this Conscious patient: fast sugar by mouth. Emergency: glucagon by injection or nasal spray. Because everyone with type 1 diabetes, and many with type 2, use insulin, hypoglycemia remains the big problem, and every patient is taught to recognize the signs early. A patient who notices them can take high-sugar foods or drinks: orange juice, regular soda or glucose tablets. In an emergency, glucagon is the drug of choice, which raises glucose from the liver. It comes as a dry powder kit mixed with water for injection, a stable liquid for injection, or nasal glucagon, given the way nasal naloxone is. 11 Diagnosis and physiology: A1C and glucose cutoffs, prediabetes, GLUT4, complications Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank So an A1C of 6.5 percent or higher, a fasting glucose of 126 milligrams per deciliter or higher, a 2-hour glucose tolerance value of 200 or higher, or a random glucose above 200. Prediabetes is an A1C of 5.7 to 6.4 percent or a fasting glucose of 100 to 125. A random glucose isn't very reliable on its own, because it depends on when the person last ate. Also flagged in class Expect this lecture to carry many of the 45 new-material questions: know every class's mechanism and main side effects, and insulin, metformin, the GLP-1 agonists and the SGLT2 inhibitors in depth. Mealtime coverage needs a fast insulin (rapid analogs or regular); NPH starts in 2 to 4 hours and glargine is basal. Insulin, sulfonylureas and meglitinides cause hypoglycemia; the rest rarely do on their own. For every class, know its hypoglycemia risk and its weight effect. Metformin is first-line unless a comorbidity (weight, heart failure, cardiovascular disease) points to a GLP-1 agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor. eGFR below 30 means stop metformin. Secretagogues fail when beta cells are gone (for example when C-peptide is absent). Absent C-peptide in a patient on insulin means no insulin of their own. Prioritize insulin, GLP-1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors and metformin, and situational choices among them. Obesity plus new type 2 diabetes points to a GLP-1 agonist such as semaglutide. Heart failure plus diabetes points to an SGLT2 inhibitor; dapagliflozin is FDA approved to treat heart failure. Regular insulin and NPH can be bought without a prescription. Diagnosis needs two agreeing results: A1C 6.5% or more, fasting glucose 126 or more, OGTT 200 or more, random above 200. You can skip Skip insulin dose arithmetic; know the preparations, their timing and basal versus bolus use. For the TZDs, know PPAR-gamma (a nuclear receptor) and the effects, not the gene details. Know acarbose and pramlintide in outline: mechanism, the main adverse effect, and when they cause hypoglycemia. Colesevelam: barely absorbed, binds other drugs, can raise triglycerides; bromocriptine is only listed. Don't memorize the SGLT2 warnings drug by drug; know the class's infections, polyuria and hypotension, and the boxed warning for amputation.
